newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan funds, traders cautious about Thai outlook.
newsitem.headline: Japan funds, traders cautious about Thai outlook.

text.p: Signs that Thailand will seek international help with its financial crisis were welcomed by Japanese fund managers and currency dealers, but they said it will take time for the country to restore investor confidence.
The Thai baht regained some ground on news earlier this week that Thailand's government was studying whether a standby credit line from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was necessary.

"Seeking IMF loans would be a good step, but it is unlikely to boost the baht significantly from current levels. The currency market has already largely factored it in," said a Japanese bank dealer specialising in Asian currencies.
After Thailand's surprise move on July 2 to float its currency, the baht lost more than 20 percent of its value against the dollar, hitting a record low of 32.70 per dollar on July 24.
The baht was quoted around 31.800/200 per dollar in the domestic market early on Friday.
"The baht's upside will probably remain heavy in the short run and another downward move cannot be ruled out," the Japanese bank dealer said.
"Thailand's private sector is burdened with heavy foreign currency-denominated borrowing. The crisis will not be over until hedge selling by Thai firms is out of the way," he added.
Fund managers also said the time was not yet ripe for aggressive accumulation of Thai stocks.

"Many Thai firms hold a large amount of foreign currency-denominated loans, so the recent baht plunge is expected to force these firms to lower their earnings estimates. The stock market has not fully factored this in yet," said Susumu Fujikawa, portfolio manager at Nikko Securities Investment Trust and Management Co Ltd.
Of Thailand's $89.8 billion in foreign debt, $73 billion is in the form of commercial credits, Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said during a trip to Tokyo two weeks ago.
"Export-oriented firms are expected to benefit from a weaker baht, but many of these shares have been bought up quite a bit and their valuation is already at a very high level," Fujikawa said.
Fujikawa said his company's weighting in Thailand was zero before the baht float, but he is now considering gradually accumulating selective stocks.
"Our stance now is to buy if there are export-oriented stocks with attractive valuations," he said.

Thailand's SET share index fell to a low for the year of 457.97 points after the resignation of Amnuay Viravan as finance minister on June 19, but it climbed back above 600 after the baht float, and received a further boost this week from the IMF news. On Thursday the key index closed at 665.62.

Fund managers and currency dealers said they will be carefully monitoring Thailand's current account data in the coming months to see if the baht's de facto devaluation helps Thai exports regain their competitive edge.
"At this point, it is still uncertain whether the devaluation will actually improve the country's current account," said the Japanese bank dealer.
Thailand's current account deficit narrowed to a preliminary 22.8 billion baht in May from a deficit of 38.0 billion baht in April, the Bank of Thailand said on Thursday.
Meanwhile, the country's foreign reserves fell to $32.4 billion in June from $33.3 billion in May, the central bank said.
